title: Choosing Settlement Instruments for Tokenized Asset Transactions
subtitle: Bank money, tokenized deposits, stablecoins and central-bank settlement in a supporting role
abstract: TSP-01 is not a monetary-policy research site. It must nevertheless identify which asset discharges a transaction, what legal claim the payee receives, and when funds become usable. A tokenized receipt can be funded in commercial-bank money, a tokenized deposit, a private stablecoin or an institutionally accessible central-bank settlement arrangement. This briefing offers an instrument-selection method grounded in asset lifecycle requirements.

evidence.heading: Several monetary instruments can support one asset token
evidence.body: The BIS Annual Economic Reports 2025 and 2026 distinguish central-bank money, commercial-bank liabilities and stablecoins as different monetary forms and explore how they might interact in programmable arrangements. The BIS/CPMI tokenisation framework makes this choice a part of the transaction design rather than an automatic consequence of the asset token standard. The financial question is not whether the settlement asset is on-chain, but whether its transfer discharges the obligation under the transaction contract.

evidence.heading: Prototype architectures are not required choices
evidence.body: BIS Project Agorá tested a programmable wholesale platform integrating bank deposits and central-bank reserves, while Helvetia studied tokenized asset settlement in a wholesale CBDC setting. These experiments illustrate feasible design options, not a mandate to replace all bank payment systems or issue a new currency. An asset platform should avoid making its legal and servicing layers dependent on any one payment token unless there is a deliberate governance reason.

architecture.heading: Instrument decision table
architecture.body: For each settlement instrument compare the issuer liability, eligible users, redemption rights, source of finality, transfer restrictions, supported currencies, operating hours, counterparty concentration and off-ramp. A stablecoin balance under a self-custodied wallet is not automatically the same claim as a credited insured bank deposit. A central-bank reserve transfer may have strong settlement properties but is generally accessible only through the relevant system's eligibility and operational conditions.

architecture.heading: Asset-payment interface
architecture.body: Define a PaymentLeg with amount, currency, payer, payee, instrument, settlement network, irrevocability criterion, expiry, fees and proof reference. A DeliveryLeg identifies the valid asset right being delivered. A coordinator links the two with conditional acceptance, cancellation and exception states. Recording chain confirmation without evidence that the payee received its contractual money obligation leaves the DvP assertion incomplete.

architecture.heading: Keep stablecoin research at the relevant boundary
architecture.body: Reserve management, bank-deposit substitution, monetary sovereignty, issuer portfolio dynamics and detailed macroeconomic consequences belong in a companion money edition. For TSP-01, retain only what changes a tokenized asset investment or trading decision: redeemability, credit exposure, liquidity availability, currency conversion, legal finality and operational reliability.

case.title: Illustrative security purchase with alternative payment legs
case.setup: An investor buys a tokenized security for USD 200,000, with final delivery required only after accepted payment. These routes are conceptual; fees and eligibility are not assumed identical.
rows: Bank confirmation and final beneficiary credit
Released only against selected acceptable payment leg
case.formula: Economic payment completion must be defined by the contract, not inferred from technology: AcceptedPayment = ValidInstrument ∧ FinalityEvidence ∧ BeneficiaryUsabilityCondition.
case.interpretation: The same securities receipt may use different settlement arrangements. Asset rights and custody should remain well-defined regardless of the chosen funding rail.

risks: Counterparty receives an asset token but a stablecoin transfer was not acceptable legal payment.
Specify acceptable instrument and governing contract.
Settlement token arrives, yet beneficiary cannot promptly convert to usable local money.
Test spendability, off-ramp and liquidity under stress.
Bank and token payment instructions each execute after a timeout.
Exclusive payment-leg IDs and idempotent finality records.
tests: Use one securities delivery with four simulated payment legs and verify which satisfy contractual discharge.
Measure time to usable beneficiary funds rather than ledger confirmation time alone.
Simulate a stablecoin suspension and bank payment outage without changing the asset-rights record.
conclusion: Monetary infrastructure should be treated as an interface to tokenized capital markets. The instrument chosen matters for finality, credit exposure and liquidity, but it should not dominate TSP-01's research agenda.

title: Redemption and Spendability Boundaries in Asset-Backed Transactions
subtitle: Why token receipt, cash availability and discharge must be measured separately
abstract: In an asset sale or redemption, the seller's goal is normally not to receive a particular blockchain event but to obtain spendable proceeds under the agreed currency and contract. This briefing distinguishes token redemption, intermediary acceptance, commercial-bank credit, liquidity access and final accounting discharge. Deep stablecoin macroeconomics are intentionally outside scope.

evidence.heading: Stablecoin transfers cannot be equated to settled cross-border payments
evidence.body: BIS Working Paper 1385 compares cross-border costs among bank, fintech and stablecoin rails using harmonized all-in cost measures. Its framing makes clear why funding, conversion, withdrawal and intermediary services matter alongside network transfer. TSP-01 should preserve that insight without treating stablecoins as the subject of an independent macroeconomic programme.

evidence.heading: Redeemability is different from transferability
evidence.body: The BIS 2026 monetary report discusses trade-offs in digital-money arrangements, including stablecoins. An instrument may move quickly on a blockchain while access to issuer redemption, bank processing or another currency is limited. For a custody-backed stock receipt, this distinction also appears when a user can sell a token continuously but cannot redeem it into underlying shares outside specified cut-offs.

architecture.heading: Define three endpoints
architecture.body: The first endpoint is transfer confirmation: an amount of a digital instrument moved under ledger rules. The second is contract settlement: the transaction counterparty has received the agreed form of payment with legal discharge. The third is economic usability: a beneficiary can apply the funds for its intended purpose. These can coincide or be hours apart; report all three rather than compressing them into a single label 'instant'.

architecture.heading: Cost and timing reconciliation
architecture.body: The payment process must account for initial principal, spread, network fees, intermediary fees, conversion and tax where applicable. Assign a unique beneficiary entitlement ID, expected net amount, applied FX quote, final amount and usable-funds timestamp. Once a payout is complete, reconcile token burn or asset delivery separately from cash receipt so a missing off-ramp does not disappear from reporting.

architecture.heading: Stress requires failure-aware states
architecture.body: Model on-chain funds available but off-ramp suspended; bank creditor account frozen; FX liquidity exhausted; payment accepted but proceeds blocked. The issuer should identify whether a claimant holds money, a receivable against a payment agent, or an unpaid distribution obligation, and should not represent any of these conditions as a completed cash return.

case.title: Illustrative redemption of a USD 50,000 receipt position
case.setup: A holder redeems units for USD 50,000 gross. In one modeled route a bank payment carries USD 35 fees; in another a token-based payout has USD 2 network fee, 0.12% conversion spread and USD 20 off-ramp charge. These figures are synthetic.
rows: $49,965 net, subject to final beneficiary credit
Token transfer confirmed, not yet local bank cash
$49,918 net if all costs borne by holder
May differ between rails and jurisdictions
case.formula: Synthetic net bank route = $50,000 − $35 = $49,965. Synthetic digital route = $50,000 − $2 − $60 − $20 = $49,918. Route choice depends also on risk, execution certainty and timing.
case.interpretation: Do not generalize these illustrative fees into market averages. They show why network costs are not sufficient for comparing settlement alternatives.

risks: Dashboard marks token delivery as paid even while off-ramp remains pending.
Three-endpoint status, beneficiary acknowledgment and unpaid payable.
Conversion rate changes before fiat delivery, creating funding shortfall.
Execution limits, lock expiry and clear cost allocation.
Failed acknowledgment triggers a duplicate payout.
Idempotent payment identifiers and beneficiary/issuer reconciliation.
tests: Report time to transfer, time to legal settlement, and time to spendable proceeds separately under two payout routes.
Reconcile paid, unclaimed and pending proceeds to outstanding redemption liabilities.
Simulate an interrupted off-ramp and verify that holder rights and cash payables are not silently extinguished.
conclusion: For TSP-01, settlement instruments matter where they affect tokenized asset rights and completed capital returns. A future monetary-systems edition can study reserve economics and systemic monetary effects independently.
